title: Andrew Youn's $7,000 Test With About 40 Farm Families in Bungoma
dek: In early 2006 an MBA student put his own savings into a farm-credit trial in western Kenya, and the first families changed the plan.

story.event: Testing a class business plan with about 40 farm families in Bungoma
story.summary: In 2005 Andrew Youn, a Kellogg MBA student, met two neighbouring farmers in Bungoma, western Kenya, whose maize harvests differed about fourfold, and wrote a business plan to supply seed, fertiliser and training on credit. In early 2006 he put $7,000 of his own money into a pilot with about 40 families, run day to day with co-founder John Gachunga; early repayment in harvested maize was later replaced with cash. One Acre Fund served more than 500 families within about 18 months and 5.9 million households in 2025.
paragraphs: In the summer of 2005 Andrew Youn, an MBA student at Northwestern University's Kellogg School of Management, extended an internship in South Africa with a trip to western Kenya. In Bungoma he met two neighbouring farmers. One family, he later said, had grown about two tons of maize on an acre, enough for the year; the family across the road had managed half a ton from the same size of plot and had lost a child. The difference, as he saw it, was seed, fertiliser and training. "I felt like someone had just struck me on the head and said, 'Fix this, you idiot,'" he told the Stanford Social Innovation Review.

That autumn he turned the idea into a business plan for a Kellogg entrepreneurship course: seed, fertiliser and training on credit, repaid after the harvest. Finished by December 2005, it went on to win four national competitions. Rather than leave it as coursework, Youn flew back to Kenya and put $7,000 of his own money into a test with about 40 families. Raising money was new to him; the first time he asked a classmate, Matt Forti, for $20 a month, he later wrote, "I was so nervous that my voice was shaking."

The pilot opened in early 2006. John Gachunga, a Kenyan project manager who joined that year as co-founder, ran the daily work: enrolling farmers, hiring staff, keeping the accounts. Part of the plan did not survive the fields. Farmers first repaid in kind, with some of their maize, which kept field officers busy supervising harvests, shelling and drying. Gachunga later said it also raised a moral question, because taking away part of their harvest "defeated that purpose." Farmers had other income, so the team switched to cash.

By May 2006, with graduation days away and, by Kellogg's account, no job offer to fall back on, Youn chose the farms. A grant from Kellogg's Levy Institute and a two-year Echoing Green fellowship let him move to Kenya full time, and he skipped his own graduation to fly to Bungoma. Within about eighteen months One Acre Fund was serving more than 500 families, and by 2010 some 30,000 in Kenya and Rwanda. In 2025 it served 5.9 million farming households in ten countries.

quote.text: The farmer is covetous of his dollar, and with reason. It is no waif to him. He knows how many strokes of labor it represents. His bones ache with the day's work that earned it.
quote.source_title: The Conduct of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #39827
quote.connection: In a business plan, repayment is a line in a spreadsheet. Emerson writes from the farmer's side of the ledger, where every coin carries the ache of the day that earned it. That weight is what Bungoma's first families made the team feel when they stopped taking repayment out of the harvest itself.

reflection: A plan can be finished, and even admired, long before it has met the people it is for. Youn's won four competitions; it took about forty families in Bungoma to show that one of its rules, repayment in maize, worked against the very thing the plan was meant to do. Nobody could have seen that from a business-school classroom.

You will have rules of your own, at work and at home, that made sense when you wrote them down. The useful question is not whether they are clever but what they cost the person who has to live with them, counted, as Emerson would put it, in that person's own aching hours.
invitation: Pick one rule or routine you ask of someone else, a form, a deadline or a habit at home, and ask the person who follows it what it costs them. Listen without defending it.

research_notes: Pilot size: the Stanford Social Innovation Review (2011) and Northwestern Magazine (2007) both say 40 families; the Kellogg School's 2026 anniversary article (and Wikipedia, uncited) say 38. The story says 'about 40'. Other early totals disagree more widely and are not used: NextBillion/GOOD says 300 families in 2006, and PBS NewsHour (2012) says 5,000 in 2006, which looks like an error. Pilot date: SSIR says One Acre Fund opened in January 2006; Wikipedia says February 2006; the story says 'early 2006'. Sequence: Northwestern Magazine (2007) says that at the end of the academic term Youn flew back to Kenya and funded the 40-family demonstration; Kellogg (2026) separately describes a decision in May 2006, days before graduation, after which he skipped the ceremony to fly to Bungoma and 'launch' One Acre Fund full time. The story treats these as two steps (a winter pilot, then the full-time move) and attributes the May decision and the 'no job offer' detail to Kellogg. The two-farmer scene rests on Youn's own recollection, given slightly differently over the years (two tons versus half a ton in SSIR; 'four times less' in NextBillion; 'four times as much food' in his Northwestern essay); SSIR says the child died of starvation, the others only that a child was lost, and the story uses the latter. Northwestern Magazine (2007) opens with a different scene, Youn waking in a farmer's hut; it is not used. Sponsor a Farmer: SSIR says $20 supported a family for a month, Kellogg says it was the projected cost of serving a family for a year; the story mentions only the $20-a-month request. The switch from in-kind to cash repayment is from Gachunga's 2021 interview and is not dated; Northwestern Magazine (2007) still describes crop repayment, so the story places it after the first seasons without a date. Gachunga's interview says he met Youn in 2006; Echoing Green calls him co-founder of the Kenya programme. The Kellogg article and the Northwestern essay are institutional publications of Youn's university, so they are treated as close to the founder rather than independent; each pivotal claim is also backed by SSIR, NextBillion, One Acre Fund or Echoing Green. The SSIR print PDF (ssir.org/images/articles/2011SU_WhatWorks_Binns.pdf) has the same text; the HTML article is cited because the verifier can read it. Emerson's sentence is from the essay 'Wealth' and concerns a New England farmer's dollar; it is applied here by analogy.
